hints: Look closely at what is the same and what is different in the two displayed structures, focus on connectivity versus spatial arrangement.
Notice the C=C bond nearest the $\text{CH}_2\text{OH}$ group has the same two groups attached in both molecules, but they are arranged differently in space.
Think about which type of stereoisomerism occurs when rotation is restricted around a double bond and the two key groups swap sides.
walkthrough:
**Check the connectivity**

First, let's be good detectives. Count the atoms and trace the skeleton in both geraniol and nerol.

Both have the same carbon chain, the same two C=C double bonds in the same places, and the same $\text{-OH}$ functional group on the same carbon. So the connectivity is identical.

**Zoom in on the key double bond**

Now look at the C=C bond on the right, the one attached to $\text{CH}_2\text{OH}$. Each C of that double bond has two different groups.

Left C has $\text{CH}_3$ and $\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2$- , right C has $\text{H}$ and $\text{CH}_2\text{OH}$. Because rotation about C=C is restricted, different spatial arrangements are possible.

**Compare cis and trans arrangement**

In geraniol, the two bulky carbon groups ($\text{CH}_3$ on top and $\text{CH}_2\text{OH}$ on top right) are on the same side of the double bond. The two H atoms are also together below.

In nerol, they have swapped. $\text{CH}_2\text{OH}$ is now below the double bond, opposite to $\text{CH}_3$. This same side versus opposite side difference around C=C is exactly geometrical (cis-trans) isomerism.

options.A: Chain isomerism means a different arrangement of the carbon skeleton, such as straight versus branched. Here both molecules have the identical 10-carbon chain with methyl branches in the same places, so this is not chain isomerism.
options.B: Correct. The connectivity is the same but the spatial arrangement around the restricted C=C bond differs. Geraniol is the trans (E) form and nerol is the cis (Z) form with respect to the $\text{CH}_2\text{OH}$ and $\text{CH}_3$ groups. This is geometrical (cis-trans) stereoisomerism.
options.C: Optical isomerism requires a chiral centre (usually a carbon with four different groups) giving non-superimposable mirror images. Neither molecule has a chiral centre, and these two structures are not mirror images, they differ only by cis-trans arrangement.
options.D: Positional isomerism means the same skeleton but the functional group or double bond is in a different position. Here the $\text{-OH}$ group and both double bonds are in exactly the same positions in the chain, only their geometry in space changes.
